Copy these measurements What the numbers mean The spine width is the thickness of the stacked text block plus whatever the binding adds. The cover artwork size is what your designer or your PDF export actually needs: back cover, spine and front cover laid out as one flat sheet, with bleed added on all four edges so the trim can wander a millimetre without showing white. Spine width is calculated as (page count ÷ 2) × sheet thickness + binding allowance. Sheet thickness comes from the paper’s grammage and its bulk: thickness in mm = gsm × bulk ÷ 1000, with bulk taken as 1.25 cm³/g for uncoated stock and 0.94 for coated matte. That is why 130 gsm matte comes out barely thicker than 100 gsm bond — coating compresses the fibres, so a heavier coated sheet can be thinner than a lighter uncoated one. content.title: How thick will my book be? Page count to physical inches
content.content: How thick will my book be? Page count to physical inches Book Designer AI｡The short answer: your book's thickness is just page count × the paper factor. At both KDP and IngramSpark that factor is 0.002252" per page on white paper and 0.0025" on cream. So a 300-page book is about 0.68" thick on white and about 0.75" on cream. That same number is your spine width, which is why the cover wrap depends on it exactly. Full table below. The one formula you need There is no mystery to how thick a paperback comes out. It is a single multiplication: thickness (inches) = page count × paper factor The paper factor is a fixed per-page thickness set by the printer. At the two most common print-on-demand platforms, the numbers are the same as each other: Paper Factor per page Where White 0.002252 inches KDP and IngramSpark Cream 0.0025 inches KDP and IngramSpark That is the whole calculation. Plug in your final page count, multiply, and you have the physical thickness of the text block, which for a paperback is also the width of the spine. The worked table Here is what common page counts translate to in real inches, on both papers, using the factors above: Page count White (× 0.002252) Cream (× 0.0025) 100 0.225" 0.250" 200 0.450" 0.500" 300 0.676" 0.750" 500 1.126" 1.250" 800 1.802" 2.000" Two things jump out. First, cream is consistently thicker, and the gap widens as the book grows: at 800 pages the same manuscript is about two-tenths of an inch fatter on cream than on white. Second, thickness scales in a straight line with page count, so once you know your final page count the number is exact, not an estimate. Why the number actually matters This is not trivia. The thickness of your book drives four practical things. 1. Spine text legibility A thin spine cannot carry readable text. As a rough guide, spines under about 0.25 inches are left empty by professional designers, because on a narrow spine the title drifts visibly with normal binding tolerance and an off-center spine reads as an error to anyone browsing a shelf. From the table, that threshold lands around 110 pages on white and 100 on cream. Below that, plan on a blank spine. Each printer also enforces its own minimum page count before it allows any spine text at all, so check your printer's rule alongside this rule of thumb. 2. Shelf presence Thickness is what a browser sees edge-on in a bookstore or library. A book too thin to show a legible spine is essentially invisible on a shelf, seen only face-out. A book of healthy thickness announces itself from the side. This is one more reason very short books sometimes benefit from a smaller trim or slightly more generous typesetting: a little more thickness buys real shelf visibility. 3. Shipping weight More pages and thicker paper mean a heavier book, and weight feeds directly into what it costs you to ship copies and, in some cases, into print cost. Cream's extra thickness is also extra weight. None of this is a reason to avoid cream when your book calls for it, but it is worth knowing that the paper choice touches the scale as well as the spine. 4. The cover wrap depends on it exactly This is the big one. Your paperback cover is one flat file wrapping the back, spine, and front. The spine panel has to match the physical thickness of the printed book almost exactly, or the wrap misaligns and the file gets rejected. Because the spine equals page count times paper factor, any change to either number, a reflow that shifts the page count or a switch between cream and white, changes the spine and can break a cover that was already designed. Lock the page count and the paper before the cover is built, and the wrap is computed once and stays correct. The hardcover exception Everything above is paperback math. Hardcover is different and you should not use this formula for it. A hardcover case laminate cover adds the thickness of the cover boards on top of the text block, and printers compute hardcover spines from their own stepped tables rather than the per-page factor. The values snap to set steps and do not track the paperback multiplier. For any hardcover, take the spine from the printer's own template generator or calculator rather than deriving it from the page-count math here. Our companion guide on book spine width covers the hardcover tables in detail.

content.title: How will you measure the thickness of a page of your book? The thickness of 100 sheets of paper is 10mm. Find the thickness of one sheet.
content.content: How will you measure the thickness of a page of your book? The thickness of 100 sheets of paper is 10mm. Find the thickness of one sheet. StudyX｡Ideas for Solving the Problem Indirect Measurement: Since a single page is very thin, directly measuring it with a ruler or caliper will be inaccurate. We can measure the thickness of a stack of pages and then divide by the number of pages. Thickness Calculation: The thickness of one sheet can be found by dividing the total thickness of the sheets by the number of sheets. Calculation Steps Step 1: Calculate the thickness of one sheet. Given that the thickness of 100 sheets is 10 mm, we can find the thickness of one sheet by dividing the total thickness by the number of sheets. Thickness of one sheet = Total thickness / Number of sheets Thickness of one sheet = 10 mm / 100 Thickness of one sheet = 0.1 mm Final Answer To measure the thickness of a page of a book, I would measure the thickness of a large number of pages (e.g., 100 or 500), and then divide the total thickness by the number of pages. The thickness of one sheet of paper is 0.1 mm. Highlights Measuring a small thickness directly is prone to error. Measuring a larger quantity and then dividing provides a more accurate result. Ensure the units are consistent throughout the calculation. In this case, the thickness was given in millimeters (mm), and the answer is also in millimeters (mm).

content.title: How Are Hardcover Book Dimensions Decided?
content.content: How Are Hardcover Book Dimensions Decided? Xinyi Printing｡ Larger hardcover books require a wider case extension to better protect the inner pages and maintain balanced proportions on the shelf. As a general guideline: Hardcover books under 400 pages usually use an overhang of around 0.125″ (3 mm) on each open side. Books between 400 and 800 pages often require a slightly larger overhang of approximately 0.1875″ (4.5 mm). Very thick hardcovers over 800 pages may use an overhang of 0.25″ (6 mm) or more, depending on the binding structure and board thickness. Because spine construction, paper type, and binding style can all affect the final case dimensions, it’s always recommended to confirm the exact overhang specifications with your printer before production begins. Example (US Trade 6″×9″, 300 pages) Let’s assume: Trim size: 6″ wide × 9″ high Spine width (estimated): 0.7″ (see Section 4 for calculation) Overhang: 0.125″ on each side Case Cover Width = (6″ × 2) + 0.7″ + 0.125″ + 0.125″ = 12″ + 0.7″ + 0.25″ = 12.95″ Case Cover Height = 9″ + 0.125″ + 0.125″ = 9.25″ So your final case cover size is 12.95″ wide × 9.25″ high. This is the dimension you should use for your cover artwork’s trim size (before adding bleed). Hardcover Overhang Recommendations The amount of hardcover overhang typically increases as the book becomes thicker. Larger and heavier books often require a slightly wider case extension to improve durability, protect page edges, and maintain balanced proportions. As a general production guideline: Book Thickness (pages) Recommended Overhang Up to 400 pages Around 0.125″ (3 mm) 400–800 pages Around 0.1875″ (4.5 mm) Over 800 pages Around 0.25″ (6 mm), depending on binding structure Actual overhang dimensions may vary depending on the hardcover binding style, board thickness, and printer production standards. How Spine Width Affects Hardcover Dimensions Estimating spine thickness accurately is essential for hardcover size – especially if the spine includes text or a graphic. Since you won’t have a printed book block before the cover is designed, use the following method. Spine Thickness (mm) = (Total Pages ÷ 2) × Paper Thickness (mm per sheet) Paper Thickness Reference Table Paper Type GSM Thickness per sheet (mm) Thickness per sheet (inches) Coated matte/gloss Paper 80 0.10 0.0040 Uncoated offset (premium) Paper 100 0.12 0.0047 Coated matte/gloss Paper 128 0.11 0.0043 Coated matte/gloss Paper 157 0.14 0.0055 Coated matte/gloss Ppaer 200 0.18 0.0071 Example Calculation Scenario: 300 pages 80 gsm uncoated paper (0.10 mm per sheet) Spine thickness = (300 ÷ 2) × 0.10 mm = 150 × 0.10 = 15.0 mm (approx. 0.59″) How Binding Styles Affect Hardcover Size? Different hardcover binding styles can slightly change the final cover dimensions. Square-back hardcovers use the standard calculation formula directly. Rounded-spine hardcovers usually require a slightly wider spine allowance to account for the curved shape. Dust jackets are printed slightly larger than the hardcover case to allow for wrapping and folding around the boards. Because the binding structure affects the final measurements, it’s always best to confirm the exact cover template with your printer before finalizing the artwork. In brief A 100-page paperback at 8.5×8.5 inch on KDP has a spine width of 0.225 in (5.72 mm) on white paper, or 0.250 in (6.35 mm) on cream. Wide enough for spine text. Last reviewed by Robert Prime — May 2026 Quick answer: For a 100-page paperback at 8.5" × 8.5", the spine width is 0.225" (5.72 mm) on white paper, or 0.250" (6.35 mm) on cream. Spine is 0.225" wide — clears KDP’s 0.2" minimum for spine text. Different page count or paper? The KDP Spine Width Calculator does every trim size and paper type, and gives you the full wrap-around cover dimensions including bleed. UK note: UK-specific considerations apply — ISBN purchases go through Nielsen (not Bowker), VAT rules differ from the US (both print books and ebooks are zero-rated (ebooks since 1 May 2020)), and GDPR applies to any email/customer data. The cover needs three panels — back cover, spine, front cover — plus bleed on every outer edge. content.content: Pages per Inch Calculator Case Paper｡Pages per Inch Calculator Inching towards your printing goals? Our paper calculator can speed things up! PPI PPI Estimate the number of pages per inch of paper (PPI), based on the sheet’s thickness (caliper). SHOW FORMULA 2 / Caliper = Pages per Inch (PPI) The pages per inch (PPI) for 100# gloss coated cover with an average caliper of .0095 inches per sheet is: 2 / .0095 = 211 PPI Caliper Result: Calculate Clear What is Pages Per Inch and What Does It Measure? So, you’ve landed on our pages per inch calculator and now you are wondering what it’s for. Pages per inch, as you may have guessed, tells you how many pages fit within a stack of pages that is one inch tall. Why does that matter? Most often, this measurement allows printers to figure out the thickness of a stitched book based on the thickness of one sheet of the type of paper they are using. If you are a book printer trying to decide which paper you need to buy for printing your book, knowing the PPI will help you determine how it will impact the binding aspect of your finished book. Pages per inch can be abbreviated PPI, but keep in mind that this abbreviation can also refer to Pixels per inch, a measure of image resolution that is important in digital design and printing. We’re a paper company whose customers include commercial printers, so our PPI calculator is for determining pages per inch as you plan which paper you want to order. How Our Pages per Inch Calculator Can Help You Using our pages per inch calculator can help you figure out which of our products fit your needs best. In particular, if you are printing a book, knowing the PPI of the papers you are considering can help you to understand how your stitched book will turn out and compare which type of paper will give you the result you want. Our calculator can simplify the calculations to make the process easier for you. How Do I Calculate Pages Per Inch? You can use our calculator, and here’s how! To calculate PPI, you need to use the paper’s caliper, which is the measure of paper thickness. This makes sense, since pages per inch is based on the thickness of the paper. On our calculator above, just input your caliper in points, and then click, “Calculate” to get your result. That’s all there is to it! Easier than plugging in a USB cable the right way on the first try. By the way, if you also need to know your paper’s caliper, we have a helpful caliper table to help with that! As we mentioned, caliper is the measure of paper thickness (and it’s even named after the device that can measure it!) That’s definitely an important measurement to accurately understand when planning what paper you want for your printing project. What if I want to do the math myself? If you’re one of those math people, firstly, that’s awesome! Secondly, on our calculator above, you can click “Show Formula,” which is written in red above “Caliper.” When you do that, you’ll see that the formula for PPI is 2 Divided by Caliper = Pages per Inch (PPI). That’s not too tough to calculate by hand, but we want to make sure that the non-math people can also get the PPI info they need! Afterall, we believe everyone deserves a smooth paper process. Frequently Asked Questions about Pages per Inch Talking about paper is one of our favorite things to do, so let us answer all your PPI questions! How many pages are in an inch of paper? How many sheets of paper is 1 inch? These questions sound about the same, but in different words. Unsurprisingly, both of these questions have the same answer: it depends! The caliper of a sheet of paper determines its pages per inch or PPI, which is the measure of how many pages are in a stack that is 1 inch high. Different papers have different calipers, they have different pages per inch measurements. Try putting the caliper of a few different papers into our PPI calculator and see what results you get! What is the best PPI for books? Even though this looks like a question about pages per inch for the paper for printing books, it could also be a question about pixels per inch as a measure of resolution for printing. Our PPI calculator is pretty amazing, but it only calculates pages per inch. If you came by for pixels per inch, still feel free to take a look around (never know what helpful info you may find)!

content.text:
# Solution

## Setting Up the Problem

Given information:
- Paper stacking: **100 sheets per inch** → each sheet is 1/100 = **0.01 inches thick**
- Each sheet is printed on **both sides** → 1 sheet = 2 pages
- Book thickness: **1.5 inches**

## Calculation

**Step 1:** Find the number of sheets in the book.
$$\text{Sheets} = \text{Thickness} \times \text{Sheets per inch} = 1.5 \times 100 = 150 \text{ sheets}$$

**Step 2:** Convert sheets to pages (each sheet has 2 sides).
